title: A name that is a verb (Exodus 3:13–15)
hook: Moses asks God's name and hears "I AM THAT I AM"
carry: I will be what I will be

segments.voice: Yesterday, the burning bush: a fire that wouldn't burn out, and a shepherd who stopped to look. Your line was turn aside and see. What did you turn aside for? Day eighty-two.

From the bush, God tells Moses: I have seen the affliction of my people, I have heard their cry, and I'm sending you to Pharaoh to bring them out. And Moses, standing barefoot on holy ground, asks a very practical question. When I go to the Israelites and say, the God of your fathers sent me, they're going to ask me: what's his name? What do I tell them? It's the question anyone would ask. Who are you, exactly? Today: the answer, which is not quite a name.
screen: `I HAVE SEEN, I HAVE HEARD.` → `THEY WILL ASK, WHAT IS HIS NAME?` → `WHAT DO I TELL THEM?`

segments.voice: God answers: "I AM THAT I AM." And then: tell them, "I AM hath sent me unto you." In Hebrew: Ehyeh asher ehyeh. And here's the thing an English Bible can hide. Ehyeh is a verb. It comes from the Hebrew root for to be, and it's in a form that usually points forward, into the future, or into something still going on. So it can mean I am who I am. Or I will be what I will be. Or I will be there, as I will be there. The old Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917 prints I AM THAT I AM, and notes in the margin that it could also be read I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE. Moses asked for a name, like a label you can hold. What he got was more like a promise, and a mystery. The Talmud hears the promise. It says God meant: I will be with them in this trouble, and I will be with them in troubles still to come. Rashi passes that on. Other thinkers, like Maimonides, heard something about God's very being, existence itself, beyond anything we can name. Both readings stay in the tradition. Then God gives one more name, made of four Hebrew letters, which tradition links to the same root: the name Jews treat as too holy to pronounce. Instead, in prayer, they say Adonai, my Lord, and in ordinary talk, HaShem, which just means the Name. This is my name forever, God says. A name that is a verb. Read the way the Talmud reads it, it doesn't say what God is. It promises God will be there, and leaves the how open.
screen: `EHYEH ASHER EHYEH.` · `A VERB, NOT A LABEL.` · `I WILL BE WITH THEM IN THIS TROUBLE.` · `THE NAME TOO HOLY TO SAY.` · then, large: `I AM THAT I AM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit for a minute with not fully knowing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you can't pin down. A question about God, about your future, about someone you love. Notice the urge to label it, to settle it, to know. Then just let it be open. You don't have to know how it turns out. If you pray, you can hold the words I will be what I will be. If not, let the question breathe with you. The bell holds the time.
Ehyeh. I will be, or I am. The name God gives Moses from the bush: a verb, a presence, and a promise.
Your line: I will be what I will be. Today, when you want to know how something ends, leave room for what hasn't happened yet. Day eighty-two.

howItsDone: Jews do not pronounce the four-letter name of God; in prayer and Torah reading they say Adonai, and in everyday speech many say HaShem, the Name.

fork.setup: you're Moses at the bush. you're being sent to Egypt. what's the first thing you ask about God?
fork.reveal: he asks for the name the people will ask about. the answer is a verb: I AM THAT I AM, or I will be what I will be.

original.note: Hebrew: I will be what I will be, or I am that I am. from h-y-h, to be.

trapdoor: what you thought: God's name is I AM.
what it means: a verb that can mean I am, I will be, I will be there. a promise of presence more than a label.
what a scholar hears: the imperfect form ehyeh points forward. Berakhot 9b and Rashi read it as a promise; Maimonides (Guide 1:63) as pure being.

sources.quoted: I AM hath sent me unto you.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording and its marginal note ('Or, I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE'); the script cites the margin note without quotation marks. The index carry follows that note.
Maimonides, Guide 1:63 on Ehyeh as necessary existence: confirm citation.
Tetragrammaton linked to root h-y-h: a common scholarly and traditional view; confirm framing.
Customs of Adonai/HaShem: confirm; some write G-d, not addressed here.

Editor review: the closing lines no longer state theology as the narrator's own fact (now framed as the Talmud's reading); the four-letter name's link to h-y-h is now 'tradition links', not stated as etymology.
